workforce.label: Workforce

headline.text: Broad gains coexist with heavy market concentration

summary.text: Positive one-year returns cover 68.1% of companies, while the median return is 27.2% and the equal-weight return is 54.0%.
Participation is broad, but the top ten still hold 64.2% of covered market value, leaving performance concentrated despite widespread gains.

watchpoint.text: Whether positive-return breadth expands while the top-ten market-value share declines would confirm a less concentrated advance.

headline.text: Cash generation supports spending, but commitments loom larger

summary.text: Operating cash flow covers current CapEx by 1.46x, but forward commitments equal 5.16x current CapEx and cash reserves cover 1.01 years.
Loose financial conditions and low bond distress coexist with positive borrower strain, suggesting financing access is not yet the main constraint but issuer-level pressure is uneven.

watchpoint.text: A rise in debt financing alongside lower borrower strain would indicate that large forward commitments are becoming easier to fund.

headline.text: Compute expansion spans the supply chain but remains largely committed

summary.text: Announced U.S. projects span all 4 tracked critical supply-chain layers, with 17 sites and $362.0B of expected investment.

Strong output and information-processing investment growth support expansion, while lower semiconductor utilization than computer-equipment utilization suggests capacity pressure is uneven across layers.

watchpoint.text: Movement of the 17 announced sites into production would confirm that broad supply-chain commitments are becoming operating capacity.

headline.text: The disclosed development pipeline dwarfs operating capacity

summary.text: Development records carry 287.2 GW of published capacity versus 22.9 GW for operating sites, while development sites equal 0.51x operating sites.
The scale gap points to a large prospective buildout, but canonical capacity covers only 37.9% of active campus records, limiting confidence in aggregate comparisons.

watchpoint.text: Higher canonical-capacity coverage and movement of development sites into operation would strengthen evidence that the disclosed pipeline is translating into usable infrastructure.

headline.text: National connectivity depth masks substantial local gaps

summary.text: The public network includes 168 active U.S. exchange points, 90 international submarine cable systems, and at least 250 interconnection facilities.
Yet only 40 of 75 assessed population centers over 300k have an IXP, and 22 states combine data-center development with limited visible public interconnection depth.

watchpoint.text: New IXPs or interconnection facilities in the 22 low-visibility states would indicate that public connectivity is catching up with campus development.

headline.text: Large-load ambitions are outrunning the visible generation pipeline

summary.text: Published large-load campus records represent 263,644 MW, while net planned generation additions total 227.0 GW through 2030.
Commercial demand is growing faster than total retail demand, and retail prices are rising faster than either, reinforcing the importance of when planned supply actually arrives.

watchpoint.text: Faster conversion of the 227.0 GW planned pipeline into additions, alongside moderating prices, would ease the apparent power constraint.

headline.text: A vast queue offers limited assurance of timely supply

summary.text: The active queue totals 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages; historically, 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation and 75% withdrew.
A 5.0-year median path to commercial operation for 2025 completions makes interconnection timing a central constraint, even with 552.7 GW of storage in the queue.

watchpoint.text: Growth in advanced-stage capacity and a shorter completion timeline would show whether the queue is becoming a more credible source of supply.

headline.text: Drought exposure is visible; facility water use is not

summary.text: Mapped states with D2-or-worse drought contain 239.2 GW of published data-center capacity, including 81.0 GW where at least 25% of state area is affected.

Only 63 of 1,906 mapped facilities have direct water evidence, and none has quantified withdrawal or consumption records, preventing the visible drought overlap from establishing facility-level water stress.

watchpoint.text: Quantified facility withdrawal or consumption records, especially in drought-affected states, would materially improve assessment of campus-level water constraints.

headline.text: Generative AI is widespread, but daily use remains limited

summary.text: Some generative-AI use reaches 61.8% of adults age 18–64, and 54.2% report use in the prior week, but only 15.4% report daily use.
Work use at 45.2% shows substantial diffusion, while the gap with daily use suggests adoption depth still trails reach.

watchpoint.text: A sustained rise in daily use relative to overall use would confirm that experimentation is becoming habitual adoption.

headline.text: High task exposure has not produced broad hiring growth

summary.text: Only 1 tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth; power and communication construction is strongest at 0.8%, while computing infrastructure is weakest at -4.1%.
Meanwhile, 47.3% of benchmark occupations have at least 50% software-adjusted task exposure, indicating broad potential task impact without evidence here of broad employment expansion.

watchpoint.text: Broader positive employment growth across tracked channels would distinguish expanding AI-linked labor demand from task exposure alone.

headline.text: Productivity gains continue to outpace worker compensation

summary.text: Since 2020, productivity has risen 14.1% versus 4.5% for real hourly compensation, a 9.6-percentage-point gap, while the labor-share index has fallen 8.4%.
Rapid information-processing investment and substantial provider revenue coexist with economy-wide productivity growth, but these measures do not establish AI as the cause of that growth.

watchpoint.text: Faster real-compensation growth and a rising labor-share index would indicate that productivity gains are translating more broadly to workers.
